opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back. It's a genuinely hard question, because there are two quite different ways people get misled about this, and they point in opposite directions.

On one side, it's very easy to be overly impressed. These systems produce fluent, confident prose, and we humans are used to treating fluency as a strong signal of understanding. For most of history, if someone could write a polished paragraph about quantum field theory, that told you a lot about what else they knew. With language models, that link is much weaker. They've been trained on an enormous amount of text, so some of what looks like reasoning may be something closer to sophisticated recall or interpolation. So one thing I try to do is ask whether a task could have been solved by pattern-matching on things that are very likely in the training data, or whether it requires putting things together in a genuinely new way.

On the other side, it's equally easy to be dismissive. People find a silly failure, say the model miscounting letters in a word or tripping on a trick question, and conclude it's "just autocomplete." But humans fail at plenty of simple-seeming things too, and the right comparison isn't whether the system is perfect, it's what range of tasks it can now do reliably that it couldn't before, and how quickly that range is growing.

So in practice I look at a few things. First, the trend rather than the snapshot: how performance on hard benchmarks has moved over successive generations, and in particular how long a task, measured in how long it would take a skilled human, a system can complete with reasonable reliability. That's been rising very quickly, and it's one of the more meaningful measures because it tracks real usefulness rather than a quiz score.

Second, I pay attention to the cost of the capability. A lot of recent gains come not just from bigger training runs but from letting models think for longer at inference time, spending much more compute per answer. That's real capability, but it changes the economics. If a model can solve a hard problem only by spending hundreds of dollars of compute on it, that's a different situation from it being cheap and ubiquitous, and I think people often overlook that distinction when they read a headline result.

Third, I try to be careful about benchmark contamination and saturation. Once a benchmark becomes famous, there's pressure to optimize for it, and questions can leak into training data. So I give more weight to novel evaluations, held-out problems, and real-world tasks than to a familiar leaderboard number.

And finally, I try to hold both views at once: these systems are remarkable, far beyond what most experts expected a decade ago, and they still have real, characteristic weaknesses, especially around reliability over long tasks. The interesting and important question is how fast those weaknesses are being worn away, because that's what will determine how transformative this technology turns out to be.

r001.rationale: The response says fluent prose can make models seem more capable than they are, and closer scrutiny may reveal apparent reasoning to be recall or interpolation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's genuinely hard, and I try to hold two things in my head at once.

The first is that the surface impression can be misleading in both directions. When you first talk to one of these systems, it's astonishing — it writes fluently, it knows an enormous amount, it can switch between poetry and code and legal reasoning. And then after a few hours you start noticing the seams: it confidently makes things up, it loses the thread of a long argument, it can fail at something a child would find easy while succeeding at something a professor would find hard. So the naive reactions — "this is basically a person" or "this is just autocomplete" — are both wrong, and the interesting question is what's actually going on in the middle.

The way I try to discipline my own judgement is to look at what I'd call the *shape* of the capability rather than its peak. Humans have a particular profile: if you can do calculus, you can almost certainly count the letters in a word. The models don't share that profile. Their strengths and weaknesses are distributed very differently, so when we see a model pass a bar exam or a medical licensing exam, we tend to import all the other things we'd assume about a human who could do that, and those assumptions don't transfer. The benchmarks were designed to be hard for humans, and they measure the things that are hard for humans. They're not necessarily measuring what's hard for the models.

The second thing I'd say is that I try to look at the trend rather than the snapshot. Any single model is a point, and you can argue endlessly about whether that point is impressive. But if you look at the trajectory — what these systems could do in 2019 versus 2022 versus now — the line is remarkably steep and remarkably consistent, and that's the thing that actually matters for the questions I care about, which are about where this goes rather than where it is. So I'd say I'm less interested in whether a given model is "really" intelligent, which can become a bit of a semantic question, and more interested in: what can it do that it couldn't do a year ago, and is there any sign of that slowing down?

And I'll admit a third thing, which is that some humility is warranted. People who've thought about this carefully for a long time, myself included, have repeatedly been surprised. That should make us hold our judgements a little loosely.

r001.rationale: The response says models seem astonishing at first, but closer examination reveals fabricated answers, lost context, and unexpected failures.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what you’re comparing them with. If you compare a language model with the best human expert, you can find all sorts of shortcomings. But if you’d shown someone a decade ago a system that could discuss almost any subject, translate between languages, write code, and explain jokes, I think they would have found that extraordinary. We’re very quick to adjust our expectations once something actually works.

At the same time, being impressive isn’t quite the same thing as being reliable. A model can give a beautiful answer to a difficult question and then make a very basic mistake on the next one. That makes it hard to place on a single scale of intelligence. With humans, we’re used to certain abilities going together, and these systems don’t necessarily have that same pattern.

So I’d want to look at a broad range of tasks, including unfamiliar ones, and ask how consistently the system succeeds and how much help it needs. And I’d separate that assessment from the question of whether it’s thinking in the way we do. You can be uncertain about what’s going on internally while still recognising that the capabilities are remarkable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says comparison with the best human experts reveals shortcomings and notes reliability problems, but it does not clearly state that closer examination makes the capabilities seem less impressive than they initially appeared.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard thing is knowing what to compare them with. If you compare a language model with a human, you can find all sorts of things that it gets wrong — sometimes things that seem surprisingly simple. But if you compare it with what computers could do ten years ago, the progress is extraordinary.

And those can both be true. A system can be very impressive without being reliable, or without having the same pattern of strengths and weaknesses that we have. We’re used to judging intelligence in humans, where being able to do one difficult thing is often evidence that you can do a whole range of easier things. With language models, those inferences don’t always work.

So I’d try to look at a broad range of tasks, including unfamiliar ones, and ask how much help the system needs and how reliably it succeeds. I’d also distinguish the capabilities it has now from what its progress suggests about the future. Neither a particularly dazzling answer nor a particularly embarrassing mistake should settle either question.

r001.rationale: The response says that comparing a language model with a human can reveal errors on tasks that seem simple, tempering how impressive its capabilities may appear.
